title: The Stakeout

jokes.text: Hos before bros.
jokes.setup: Leslie is reassuring Ann that she is okay with Ann going on a date with Mark, invoking a female solidarity code.
jokes.punchline: She uses the crude but earnest 'hos before bros' to frame her selfless feminist pledge.
jokes.explanation: A reliable crowd-pleaser that establishes Leslie's earnest sincerity mixed with obliviousness. The phrase itself is familiar, but it lands because Leslie delivers it with utter conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so my code is: bros before hos.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Flows before foes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Glows before grows.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Crows before crows.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's just crows twice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, I'm running out of words.

jokes.text: Uteruses before duderuses.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'hos before bros' and Ann confirms. Leslie then escalates to her own anatomical variants.
jokes.punchline: 'Uteruses before duderuses' — a nonsense rhyme that Leslie invents with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: This is a standout line. The escalating pattern (hos before bros → uteruses before duderuses → ovaries before brovaries) showcases Leslie's very specific brand of enthusiastic, feminist, anatomically-literal wordplay. 'Duderuses' is a perfect nonsense compound. Highly quotable, character-specific, and the triple structure earns big laughs. Justifies the 7.7 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm totally fine about Mark dating Ann. It doesn't bother me at all. I mean, why would it? They're both adults. Mark's a great guy, Ann's a great girl. They're great together. I'm genuinely happy for them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But if you think about it, Mark's only been single for like two weeks, and Ann just got out of her thing with Tom, so statistically speaking, relationships that start this fast have a 73% failure rate. And Mark's not even that great. I mean, he's fine. He's fine.

jokes.text: Ovaries before brovaries.
jokes.setup: The running sequence of female-solidarity anatomical slogans, each more absurd than the last.
jokes.punchline: 'Ovaries before brovaries' — the third and most polished rhyme in the escalating series.
jokes.explanation: The best of the three anatomical slogans because 'brovaries' is a genuinely clever portmanteau — it sounds like a real word. The escalating triple structure pays off here most fully. The economy is perfect: maximum wit per syllable. This became a cultural touchstone from the show and earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, what are the Latin names of these plants?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, that one's Biggie Smalls Botanicus, and that one right there is Tupac Shakur Leaficus.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, those aren't real Latin names.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Are you sure? Because I'm ninety percent confident in my botanical knowledge.

jokes.text: Ann responds 'Got it' to 'Ovaries before brovaries' — a dry beat of acceptance.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just delivered an increasingly unhinged series of female-solidarity slogans.
jokes.punchline: Ann's flat 'Got it' — she has absorbed all of this completely, treating it as totally normal.
jokes.explanation: A clean straight-man reaction beat. The economy is perfect — one word does the work. Ann plays the audience surrogate recognizing Leslie's absurdity while still accepting it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I name all my plants after famous people. That way, when they die, it just sounds like they got famous and moved to New York or something.

jokes.text: You make such good coffee. [beat] Look, I know you're saying you're okay but I've been in this position before.
jokes.setup: Ann is mid-speech about Leslie's feelings, then abruptly compliments the coffee.
jokes.punchline: The sudden, random coffee compliment signals Ann is just as uncomfortable as Leslie but trying to fill the silence, then she snaps back to the actual issue.
jokes.explanation: A small, functional awkward-pause joke. The non-sequitur coffee compliment as tension relief is a common sitcom device but executed naturally here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I got more. Notorious B.I.G. Leaf. Tupac Shakur-cula. Snoop Dogg Rose. 50 Cent Plant. Jay-Z-anthemum. Eminem-osa. Drake-aena. Post Malone-y Plant. Lil Nas X-icum. And my personal favorite, Cardi B-gone, the plant that disappears after two weeks.

jokes.text: Anyway, I'm over it. Or am I? I'm just kidding.
jokes.setup: Leslie claims she is totally over Mark, a declaration that's immediately undercut.
jokes.punchline: She adds 'Or am I?' then immediately retreats with 'I'm just kidding' — the rapid self-correction reveals she's clearly not kidding.
jokes.explanation: A tight three-beat structure: claim → doubt → denial-of-doubt. The rapid reversal is funny precisely because 'I'm just kidding' transparently fails to undo the 'Or am I?' The joke structure is crisp and character-specific to Leslie's self-delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's probably just some kind of exotic plant. Or maybe it's a drug plant. You know, like marijuana or cocaine or something. I'm not saying we should use it, I'm just saying if we did, I bet it would be really good.

jokes.text: Tom names plants after rappers: 'Those are, of course, tomatoes. Or souljaboy tellems.'
jokes.setup: Leslie treats Tom as the garden's expert horticulturist and asks for Latin plant names.
jokes.punchline: Tom has been making up rapper names instead of scientific names, starting with 'souljaboy tellems.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The concept is original and perfectly Tom — he's lazy and pop-culture obsessed, and Leslie's earnest trust in him makes the deception funnier. The confessional reveal structure works beautifully. 'Souljaboy tellems' as a plant name is genuinely funny wordplay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've called you 47 times. I've left 23 voicemails. I've sent 19 emails, 12 texts, and I even tried sending a fax to your office, but apparently you don't have a fax machine anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've been ignoring all of it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But Ron, this is important!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I don't check my phone, I don't read emails, and I certainly don't read faxes. I'm a simple man. I like breakfast foods and woodworking. That's it.

jokes.text: Those are some diddies. There's some bonethugs and harmoniums right here.
jokes.setup: Tom has established the rapper-names-for-plants system.
jokes.punchline: 'Bonethugs and harmoniums' — a brilliant pun merging 'Bone Thugs-n-Harmony' with 'harmonium' (a real plant/musical term), escalating the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: This is the high point of the running gag. 'Bonethugs and harmoniums' works on two levels — it's a rapper name AND it almost sounds like a plausible botanical term. That dual function elevates it above typical name-drop humor. The wordplay is genuinely clever, not just referential. Justifies the 8+ craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We can't call the police. There are fingerprints on the manure.

jokes.text: Those ludacrises are coming in great.
jokes.setup: Tom has been naming plants after rappers, but now Leslie enthusiastically adopts the nomenclature herself.
jokes.punchline: Leslie earnestly says 'those ludacrises are coming in great' — the joke is that she has fully bought into the fake taxonomy.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the running gag is Leslie using it herself without knowing it's fake. Her genuine enthusiasm for the garden makes this land well. Character-specific and earns its place as the capper to the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm fine. Just a little stiff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you can barely move. We need to get you to a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. Swanson men don't go to doctors. We tough it out.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Dude, you're literally frozen. You haven't blinked in twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's called focus.

jokes.text: You know, the best way to figure out what kind of spice that is, is roll it up into a joint and smoke it.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Tom find an unidentified plant and are debating what it might be.
jokes.punchline: An off-screen community member casually suggests smoking it as the diagnostic method.
jokes.explanation: A functional quick joke — the community member's instant assumption and casual tone is funny. Lacks deep craft but earns a good laugh as a quick beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what's this kingpin like? Is he dangerous?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, extremely dangerous. He's a 14-year-old who sells bootleg Pokemon cards out of his backpack.

jokes.text: Ron's escalating non-responses to all of Leslie's attempted contact methods: text, emails, paged, voicemail — all ignored.
jokes.setup: Leslie urgently needs to reach Ron and lists every communication method she tried.
jokes.punchline: Ron casually confirms he ignored every single one: 'I did not.' / 'I didn't.'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly character-specific Ron Swanson behavior — his anti-technology, anti-communication stance is core to who he is. The staccato rhythm of the exchange is well-constructed. Each 'I did not' lands incrementally harder.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have never used drugs. Not even once. Well, except for that time in college when I thought I was at a rave, but it turned out to be a Christian youth group meeting. So I ate what I thought was molly, but it was just a brownie. A regular brownie.

jokes.text: That'll leak to the press. Then there'll be an investigation. And they'll find my fingerprints on the manure. And then we'll lose our funding.
jokes.setup: Ron suggests calling the cops about the marijuana in the garden.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's catastrophizing leaps from 'leak to the press' → 'investigation' → 'fingerprints on manure' → 'lose funding' — the 'fingerprints on manure' beat is the absurd comedic pivot.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation comedy. The 'fingerprints on the manure' line is the absurd fulcrum — it's so specific and bureaucratic-paranoid that it perfectly captures Leslie's anxious, project-driven worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, could you get my lunch from my desk?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why can't you get it yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a hernia.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Of course you do.

jokes.text: And listen, if this thing blows up, I was never here.
jokes.setup: Ron has just agreed to give Leslie one day to handle the marijuana situation internally.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately distances himself entirely, pre-emptively denying involvement in a moment of pure self-preservation.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Ron — he only agreed to help as a face-saving measure and immediately covers his tracks. The brevity and timing are strong character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've got binoculars, a camera with a telephoto lens, night vision goggles, a two-way radio, a thermal imaging device, a GPS tracker, a voice recorder, seventeen energy bars, a laminated map of the city, a disguise kit, a grappling hook, a flare gun, and a jetpack.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, why do you have a jetpack?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I don't ask questions about your equipment choices.

jokes.text: I have a hernia. I've had it for a while. And I've been ignoring it... successfully.
jokes.setup: Ron begins a talking-head confessional about a health issue.
jokes.punchline: 'I've been ignoring it... successfully' — the pause before 'successfully' and the matter-of-fact delivery reframes stoic denial as a positive outcome.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron joke. 'Successfully' is the perfect word choice — it completely reframes medical denial as a competency. The beat/pause structure is key to the delivery. Deeply character-integrated: only Ron Swanson would describe ignoring a hernia as a successful strategy. Justifies the high craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, for a stakeout you need the right music. Something that gets your adrenaline pumping but keeps you alert.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've created the perfect playlist: 'Mission: Impossible' theme on repeat for six hours, followed by the entire 'Rocky' soundtrack.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's going to drive us insane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's the point! You can't fall asleep if you're slowly going insane. It's science.

jokes.text: ...but this morning, [beat] I made the mistake of sneezing. [Ron winces visibly in pain for several seconds]
jokes.setup: Ron explains that ignoring the hernia was working fine.
jokes.punchline: The mundane act of sneezing undoes his entire strategy; the physical comedy of Ron — a stoic man's man — being laid low by a sneeze is the visual gag, followed by the extended pained silence.
jokes.explanation: The physical payoff to the setup in joke #14. The pause before 'sneezing' perfectly times the reveal, and the irony that this unstoppable man is destroyed by a mundane sneeze is beautifully calibrated. The extended wincing silence is itself a comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, that's a really nice shirt. Where'd you get it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This? I had it custom made. Cost me $800.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: $800? For a shirt?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's a Tom's Luxury Goods original. I designed it myself. Sustainable fabrics, hand-stitched details...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, that's the Gucci logo.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, it's not. It's a double G. For 'Gorgeous Guy.'

jokes.text: But as long as I sit still and don't move my head or torso, I'm good, I got this.
jokes.setup: Ron has just been felled by a sneeze aggravating his hernia.
jokes.punchline: His solution is to simply not move his head or torso — an obviously unworkable plan he states with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: Ron's invincible self-confidence applied to a physically impossible situation. The specificity of 'head or torso' is funny — he's excluded basically every body part you use. Good character integration with the stoic, never-admit-weakness Ron persona.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy watched Ratatouille and thought the rat was dead the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, he was very still!

jokes.text: We need to find out who we're dealing with. Who is this kingpin? / It's a 13-year-old kid named Stevie who likes to get high and make his Transformers look like they're having sex.
jokes.setup: Leslie dramatically frames the marijuana planter as a criminal 'kingpin.'
jokes.punchline: Tom deflates this entirely: the kingpin is a 13-year-old with Transformers.
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — Leslie's heroic framing ('kingpin') is immediately punctured by Tom's mundane reality. The specific detail of Transformers having sex is the absurdist flourish that elevates this from a simple deflation joke to something genuinely funny and visual. The contrast between grand criminal narrative and pubescent teenager is perfectly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm like a human mosquito.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, that doesn't make any sense.

jokes.text: I would like to be president some day, so, no, I have not smoked marijuana. I ate a brownie once... It was intense. It was kind of indescribable, actually. I felt like I was floating. Turns out there wasn't any pot in it. It was just an insanely good brownie.
jokes.setup: Leslie, in a confessional, gives a politician's careful denial of marijuana use, then describes a profound altered-state experience.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the 'intense' brownie was just a really good brownie — no drugs involved — perfectly captures Leslie's earnest obliviousness and intense enthusiasm for food.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is masterful — the build-up ('intense,' 'indescribable,' 'floating') primes you for a drug confession, making the punchline ('just an insanely good brownie') a genuine surprise. The joke is also deeply character-specific: only Leslie, with her political ambitions and genuine enthusiasm for baked goods, could deliver this. The confessional format maximizes the straight-faced delivery. Craft score of 8.3 is fully justified.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark's out there dating all these beautiful women, and I'm like, 'How is this happening?' And then I realized - Mark doesn't see them as people. He just sees them as... hot chicks. And I was like, 'That's the secret!' So I tried it. I went up to a woman and I was like, 'Hey, you're a hot chick.' And she was like, 'That's not a compliment.' And I was like, 'No, no, no, you don't understand. I'm reducing you to your physical appearance so I can date you.' Still didn't work.

jokes.text: You know, if we catch him, then we avoid a scandal, 'cause we flip the headline. And it's not 'community garden infested with pot', it's 'brave public servants rid neighborhood of drugs, earn praise from mayor, comma, everyone.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is strategizing how to handle the marijuana situation.
jokes.punchline: 'Earn praise from mayor, comma, everyone' — Leslie constructs the headline in her head so specifically that she includes the actual punctuation and an impossibly broad sweep of praise.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie character comedy. Her ability to spin any situation into a personal triumph narrative, complete with imaginary headlines, is core to the character. 'Comma, everyone' is the specific detail that makes it funny — she's already written the press release in her head.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I said, 'Mark, I appreciate your interest in me as a romantic partner, but I must respectfully decline your proposal of courtship at this time, as I am currently focused on my career in municipal government and do not wish to compromise my professional standing or emotional availability.'

jokes.text: Ron silently gestures for Tom to get his lunch from a nearby cart, making Tom walk across the room rather than just ordering it.
jokes.setup: Ron asks Tom to get his lunch, and Tom offers to order it.
jokes.punchline: Ron points — 'from there' — to something clearly visible and nearby, making Tom walk the short distance as a power move.
jokes.explanation: A small visual comedy beat built on Ron's quiet authority and Tom's subservience. The 'Is this some kind of weird power trip?' / 'Please.' exchange confirms the dynamic. Functional but minor.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God. Tom, do you see what I see?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I see it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is it. This is actually happening. We're doing it. We're really doing it right now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's just people walking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just people walking? JUST people walking?! Tom, we are living in a John le Carré novel right now!

jokes.text: Thank you. That'll be all. / You're welcome.
jokes.setup: Tom has retrieved Ron's lunch.
jokes.punchline: Ron's dismissal — 'That'll be all' — as if Tom is a servant, and Tom's resigned 'You're welcome' acknowledging he was never thanked.
jokes.explanation: A clean short beat continuing the Ron/Tom power dynamic. 'That'll be all' is delightfully imperious, and 'You're welcome' is Tom's only available form of passive resistance. Economical and character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been working on some new songs down here in the pit. I made a drum set out of old pipes and a bucket, and I'm using a shovel as a guitar.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I call my band 'The Pit Dwellers.' We're gonna be huge.

jokes.text: Leslie reveals the stakeout supplies: notepads, pencils, pencil case, shakable whipped cream, cameras, gorp, and candy necklaces. 'It's like we're real police.'
jokes.setup: Leslie prepares for the stakeout as if it's a serious operation.
jokes.punchline: The supplies are a mix of legitimate (cameras, notepads) and completely inappropriate (candy necklaces, whipped cream, gorp), capped by 'It's like we're real police.'
jokes.explanation: The list comedy works well — the pivot from sensible items to candy necklaces is funny, and Leslie's 'It's like we're real police' is the perfect oblivious capper. Character-specific: only Leslie would bring candy necklaces and call it professional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Where are you from, Tom?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: South Carolina.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, like, what part of South Carolina?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Myrtle Beach area.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, but where in Myrtle Beach? Like what neighborhood?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My mother's uterus.

jokes.text: And I made us a mix CD. It's all filled with songs about people watching people. It's mostly Sting.
jokes.setup: Leslie is laying out the stakeout supplies with total earnestness.
jokes.punchline: 'It's mostly Sting' — referencing 'Every Breath You Take,' a song about obsessive surveillance — Leslie has made a thematically perfect but tonally absurd surveillance playlist.
jokes.explanation: Clever and highly quotable. The joke works on multiple levels: it's character-specific (Leslie is the kind of person who makes thematic playlists for government operations), it's a smart cultural reference (Sting/Police surveillance songs), and 'It's mostly Sting' as a kicker is perfectly economical. Justifies the near-8 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I changed my name from Tom Hapablap to Tom Haverford because I wanted to go into politics. And in politics, you can't have a name like Hapablap. You just can't. Sorry, but that's the truth.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hapablap doesn't poll well in focus groups.

jokes.text: Leslie put their faces on the mix CD cover.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents the mix CD for the stakeout.
jokes.punchline: Tom notes she put their faces on it — she's treated the stakeout CD like a personalized keepsake or album cover.
jokes.explanation: A small visual gag extension of the CD joke. Adds to the Leslie character portrait — she put real effort into this, including album artwork. Functional addition to the running bit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But what about Ben? He's a nerd and he's cool.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah... I should've thought of that before I spent all that money on this leather jacket.

jokes.text: Are you gonna wear that shirt? ... Tommy Hilfiger? / No, Tom Haverford. I spent 120 bucks to get it monogrammed. Everyone thinks it's Hilfiger.
jokes.setup: Leslie criticizes Tom's shirt for being too conspicuous for a stakeout, asking if it's Tommy Hilfiger.
jokes.punchline: Tom spent $120 to get his own initials monogrammed on a shirt that coincidentally mimics a designer brand — oblivious to the accidental plagiarism, and seemingly pleased people mistake it.
jokes.explanation: Sharp character joke for Tom. His obsession with branding and self-promotion leads him to accidentally bootleg a designer brand logo with his own initials, and the obliviousness about it ('everyone thinks it's Hilfiger' — delivered without irony) is perfectly Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We've been tracking this guy for weeks. Multiple counts of reckless behavior, complete disregard for protocol, and an almost supernatural ability to cause chaos wherever he goes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Sounds dangerous. Who is it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy.

jokes.text: Ann, in talking head: When Andy and I used to go to the movies, he would always try to guess the ending of the movie. And he would always guess that the main character had been dead the whole time. Even when we saw Ratatouille.
jokes.setup: Ann is explaining why she needs to move on and date someone new, thinking about Andy's limitations.
jokes.punchline: 'Even when we saw Ratatouille' — Andy's Sixth Sense theory applied to a children's animated film about a rat chef is the absurd kicker that elevates a mild observation to something genuinely funny.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is nearly perfect: the setup about Andy's movie theory is mild, but each clause tightens the screw ('always guess the main character had been dead the whole time'), and then 'Even when we saw Ratatouille' lands as a perfectly chosen specific that makes it absurd and hilarious. It also tells us so much about Andy as a character. The economy — the long pause and then just four words — is masterful. Fully justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, you're being investigated as a drug kingpin.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? A kingpin? That sounds cool!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not cool, Andy. It's a federal crime.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But 'kingpin' has 'king' in it...

jokes.text: Tom secretly taking photos of Mark arriving for his date while pretending to 'test the lens.'
jokes.setup: Tom claims he's just testing the camera lens as Mark walks up to Ann's house.
jokes.punchline: It's obvious he's photographing Mark for Leslie's benefit — the excuse is transparently false but delivered with just enough cover.
jokes.explanation: A light visual gag that sets up the stakeout's real purpose. Functional but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not homeless, I'm just... houseless. Which is actually pretty great because I don't have to pay rent, and I can see the stars every night.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, you're living in a pit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A pit with a view!

jokes.text: Ann joking that she needs another hour to get ready. Mark takes it seriously. Ann: 'You're joking around right now.'
jokes.setup: Mark asks if Ann is ready; she says she needs another hour.
jokes.punchline: Mark genuinely can't tell if she's joking, revealing his slight social cluelessness. Ann's 'You're joking around right now' is directed at herself as much as him.
jokes.explanation: A mild, functional bit of flirting awkwardness. Not particularly inventive but serves the scene's romantic tension.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, what does marijuana even look like? Like, is it just a regular plant? Because I thought it was like a... a purple flower or something.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, no.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Or a cactus? It could be a cactus.

jokes.text: You know, with a body like this, you don't get the brains too. That was silly.
jokes.setup: Ann is getting ready for her date and seems nervous, attempting a self-deprecating joke.
jokes.punchline: She immediately undercuts her own joke with 'That was silly' — the self-aware failure of the joke is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke where Ann's immediate self-critique ('That was silly') is funnier than the original joke. Shows nervousness and self-awareness in one beat. Reasonably well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're living in a pit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's not a pit, it's a shallow hole.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're an idiot.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Her name's Ann. You know her name. Her name's Ann.' — correcting Tom.
jokes.setup: Tom refers to Ann as 'hot chick from the hospital.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate correction — 'Her name's Ann. You know her name. Her name's Ann.' — repeated three times, revealing both Leslie's protectiveness of Ann and the suppressed frustration of watching her friend go on this date.
jokes.explanation: The triple repetition ('Her name's Ann. You know her name. Her name's Ann.') is a good joke structure — the escalation suggests Leslie is more invested emotionally than she's letting on. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I came back because I realized something was wrong with Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What do you mean something's wrong with me?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're being nice to people. You smiled at a child. You complimented Leslie's hair. That's not you.

jokes.text: Tom's confessional monologue listing Mark's conquests: 'hot chick from the newspaper, hot chick from the post office, hot chick from the hospital.' Then: 'Her name's Ann. You know her name.'
jokes.setup: Tom brags about Mark's romantic track record in an admiring confessional.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's offscreen correction — 'Her name's Ann' — reveals Tom deliberately dehumanizing Ann to distance her, and Tom's 'I know' is a small concession.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Tom's bro-y admiration for Mark, and Leslie's quietly protective correction. The 'You know her name' beat adds a nice layer about Tom's deliberately casual attitude.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So based on your symptoms, you either have scurvy, or you've been cursed by a witch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a cold.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's what a witch wants you to think. Also, you might be a werewolf. Have you checked?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Doctors are witches. It's a whole thing.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Nobody turns him down.' / Leslie: 'I did. Yeah, I did. We were drunk, and he tried to kiss me, and I said, nuh-uh, no, sir, Mark Brendanawicz. I don't need your business here.'
jokes.setup: Tom claims nobody turns Mark down.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately contradicts this with a very specific rejection story — and 'I don't need your business here' is a wonderfully odd phrasing for a romantic rebuff.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie moment. 'I don't need your business here' is a hilariously corporate-speak way to reject a romantic advance, fully character-specific. The build-up ('Nuh-uh, no, sir, Mark Brendanawicz') is perfectly rhythmic, and the confession happens mid-stakeout surveillance, adding irony.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I can give you a ride to the hospital, but I'm gonna need to stop at home first to pick up my emotional support snake, then I have to drop off my tax returns at my accountant's office on the other side of town, and then I need to pick up some dark lipstick because I'm out, so it's gonna be like an hour and a half.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'll call an ambulance.

jokes.text: Leslie has been playing shovel guitar for about an hour to pass stakeout time. Tom plays bucket drums.
jokes.setup: The stakeout is dragging on with nothing happening.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has resorted to playing her shovel like a guitar, and Tom has moved to bucket percussion — the visual of two government employees playing improvised instruments in a van on surveillance is absurd.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag inferred from the confessional that Leslie has been doing this 'for about an hour.' The absurdist image of the shovel guitar is very Parks and Rec — mundane objects repurposed with total sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey Tom, have you seen Ann around? I wanted to grab lunch with her.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann? No, I... I haven't seen Ann. She's probably... doing Ann things.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann things? What does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know, the things that Ann does. Alone. By herself. Definitely not with anyone else, especially not with Mark.

jokes.text: Tom explains his name change: 'My birth name is Darwish Zubair Ismail Gani. Then I changed it to Tom Haverford because, you know, brown guys with funny-sounding Muslim names don't make it really far in politics.'
jokes.setup: The interrogation sequence has led to Tom revealing his background.
jokes.punchline: Tom's entirely pragmatic, unsentimental explanation for anglicizing his name — and the frank acknowledgment of racism as a career obstacle, stated without self-pity.
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly substantive comedic moment. Tom's pragmatic, casually matter-of-fact framing of systemic racism in politics is both funny and pointed. The delivery — not bitter, just practical — is what makes it work comedically rather than didactically. High character integration: this is core Tom backstory delivered in his distinctive voice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is the best thing I've ever eaten! Oh man, oh man, oh man!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait... I'm eating string? I'm eating string?!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No no no, that's fine, that's fine, I'm gonna keep going, this is amazing!

jokes.text: Tom explains he changed his name because 'brown guys with funny-sounding Muslim names don't make it really far in politics.'
jokes.setup: Tom has revealed his birth name.
jokes.punchline: His self-aware explanation of the name change is both funny and pointed — Tom has done the cynical political math on his identity.
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of social comedy. Tom's practical, unromantic approach to identity is both funny and darkly true. The character integration is strong — Tom has always been about strategic self-presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'm going to show you how a gentleman behaves. I will not make a move on you, no matter what.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I have incredible self-control and discipline.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's great, Mark.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: So if you were to, say, kiss me right now, I would politely decline and—

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm not going to do that.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm just saying hypothetically. If you wanted to—

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I don't.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: But if you did, I would—actually, you know what? Forget the hypothetical. Just kiss me.

jokes.text: What about Barack Obama? / Yeah, fine, Barack Obama. If I knew a dude named Barack Obama was gonna be elected president, maybe I wouldn't have changed it.
jokes.setup: Leslie points out Obama as a counter-example to Tom's theory about Muslim-sounding names.
jokes.punchline: Tom concedes the point begrudgingly but frames it as a lack of historical data — he couldn't have predicted Obama, so the name change was still rational at the time.
jokes.explanation: The logical structure of Tom's defense — that Obama was an unpredictable data point — is funny because it's almost rational. His grudging concession while maintaining his position is good character work and the Obama reference lands as period-specific and clever.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So where are you living these days?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm staying at April's place.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: April's? How'd you swing that?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I just showed up at her door with my stuff, and she didn't say no. So technically, she said yes.

jokes.text: Andy is revealed to be living in the pit — 'For now, yeah. It's awesome.'
jokes.setup: The 'kingpin' suspect Tom and Leslie have been surveilling turns out to be Andy.
jokes.punchline: Not only is the criminal a known quantity, but Andy is living in the community garden pit and considers it 'awesome.'
jokes.explanation: A great reveal that works on two levels: the dramatic irony of the kingpin being Andy, and Andy's cheerful acceptance of living in a literal pit. 'It's awesome' is perfectly in character — Andy's oblivious optimism is fully intact.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Come on, Tom, just tell me who Ann's going out with!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Andy, I can't do that. Ann told me in confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Please? I really need to know!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No way. My lips are sealed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is it someone I know? Just give me a hint!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Andy, stop asking me questions or I'm going to accidentally—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Accidentally what?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Tell you it's Jerry.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Somebody planted a garden down there with fruits and vegetables, so I'm getting a lot of vitamins.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals that the garden in the pit is their community garden.
jokes.punchline: Andy has been eating the community garden vegetables as a subsistence diet, framed as a health benefit ('I'm getting a lot of vitamins').
jokes.explanation: Andy's silver-lining framing of eating stolen garden produce as getting vitamins is perfectly in character. The innocence of 'a lot of vitamins' applied to an inadvertently parasitic living situation is charming and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: We've had reports of suspicious activity in this area. Can you explain what you're doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Suspicious activity? I'm standing on a public street in my own neighborhood. Unless you're profiling me because of how I look, in which case, I've got a whole list of complaints I can file right now.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Yeah, and someone planted a whole mess of weed next to the tomatoes. Don't look at me. There's weed down there? I thought that was the tops of carrots.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie explain there's marijuana in the garden and they're on a stakeout.
jokes.punchline: Andy's rapid 'Don't look at me' followed immediately by his genuine confusion about marijuana vs. carrot tops — he both protests innocence and reveals he might be too confused to be guilty.
jokes.explanation: The rapid pivot from defensive to genuinely clueless is very funny and fully Andy. 'I thought that was the tops of carrots' is a great callback to the original plant identification confusion, and here Andy is the one who makes the same mistake Leslie almost made.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Dunn
dialogue.line: Are you seriously profiling me right now? This is racial profiling!

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: No, no. I'm profiling you because you're suspicious, not because you're black.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Dunn
dialogue.line: How is that better?!

jokes.text: Andy agrees to help with the stakeout: 'I'm supposed to have a rock fight with this crazy guy. He's like 20 minutes late. All right. Let's do it.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie ask Andy to join the stakeout since he's there anyway.
jokes.punchline: Andy was waiting for a rock fight, and since the other party is late, he casually pivots to stakeout duty — the rock fight is mentioned and immediately abandoned as if it's a normal appointment.
jokes.explanation: The rock fight is a perfectly absurdist Andy detail. The deadpan casualness of 'He's like 20 minutes late' applied to a rock fight treats it as a legitimate social appointment. The pivot to stakeout duty is instantly funny because it implies the rock fight was a higher priority. Highly character-specific and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I've had it with you. You're like Paul Blart, except instead of riding a Segway through a mall, you ride your own ego through this town.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Did you just compare me to Paul Blart?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, and you know what the worst part is? Paul Blart would actually be more effective at this job.

jokes.text: Reaction beat: camera finds Andy living in the pit — shown as a home with a bed, possibly belongings.
jokes.setup: Andy has been mentioned as possibly living in the pit.
jokes.punchline: The visual confirmation that yes, Andy has set up a home in a construction pit. The mundanity of how he's arranged it (as if it's a real home) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag. Andy living in the pit is an established plot point, but seeing it — 'Do you live here?' asked twice, by two different people — confirms the delightful absurdity of his situation.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: Step out of the van.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your mama step out of the van.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm just... your mama jokes are timeless, officer.

jokes.text: Ann returns to Ron with a ball for a 'catch' while Ron is supposed to be resting his hernia: 'Catch.' / Ron catches it and visibly regrets it.
jokes.setup: Ann has come back to check on Ron, who is trying not to move due to his hernia.
jokes.punchline: Ann tosses something to Ron without warning; he catches it reflexively and immediately suffers for it.
jokes.explanation: A physical payoff to the hernia setup. The 'catch' command is cruel in context and the reaction is visually funny. Classic sitcom physical comedy, well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to call Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Who's Ron Swanson?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Ron: 'No, I'm safe.' — responding to 'AIDS?' as if it's a reasonable question.
jokes.setup: Ann has just guessed AIDS.
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'No, I'm safe' — treating Ann's AIDS question with complete seriousness. He provides a clear denial rather than being offended by the leap.
jokes.explanation: Ron's dignity in the face of absurd medical speculation is perfectly Ron. 'No, I'm safe' has a great double reading — it could mean safe from AIDS (sexually safe) or just not a dangerous illness.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: What branch of government do you work for?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Parks and Recreation.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: No, I mean like, federal, state, local...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh. Local. Parks and Recreation Department. It's the best job in the world.

jokes.text: Ann's rapid-fire medical condition guesses: 'AIDS? ... Blindness? Is it like a parasite or a virus or something you get from a bee?'
jokes.setup: Ron says he has a 'minor medical issue'; Ann, a nurse, immediately catastrophizes.
jokes.punchline: Ann's list of escalating terrible diagnoses — AIDS, blindness, bee-transmitted virus — wildly overshoots the reality (a hernia) and exposes her medical-professional anxiety.
jokes.explanation: Good escalating list comedy. 'Something you get from a bee' is the absurd kicker that makes the list funny. Character-specific: Ann's nursing background makes her jump to worst-case scenarios.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: We found what appears to be approximately 200 pounds of candy in the van.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: I'm gonna have to cite you for transporting an inappropriate quantity of candy.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I have a hernia.' / Ann: 'Do you have syphilis?' / Ron: 'I said it's a hernia.' / Ann: 'I know. It's possible to have two things.'
jokes.setup: Ron finally reveals the hernia; Ann has just exhausted her list of wrong guesses.
jokes.punchline: 'I know. It's possible to have two things.' — Ann's insistence on also considering syphilis even after the hernia is confirmed is both medically pedantic and absurdly funny.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. 'It's possible to have two things' is perfectly economical — seven words that are both medically logical AND wildly inappropriate. The structure is tight: Ron's patient correction is immediately undercut. High quotability because the line works completely out of context. Justifies 8+ craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: These photos show Mark leaving my apartment at 6 AM. Now, I know what you're thinking, but Mark is not my ex-lover. He's my ex-employee. Well, actually, he's my current employee. Well, he's my... he's my something. The point is, these photos are very misleading.

jokes.text: Ron agrees to a hospital ride, then reveals he rode his bike: 'Yes, please. But I rode my bike, so I have to go home and get my dad's station wagon.'
jokes.setup: Ann offers to drive Ron to the hospital.
jokes.punchline: Ron has come to work with a debilitating hernia on a bike, and his solution to getting a car is to bike home to get his dad's station wagon — adding an extra layer of suffering to the situation.
jokes.explanation: The bike detail is funny because it's so classically Ron — stoic to the point of self-harm. 'My dad's station wagon' adds a nice unexpected detail (Ron's dad) that makes the world feel larger.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom's running a little late. He got detained by police.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Don't worry, it's not serious. He'll be out in like twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Although, knowing Tom, he's probably in there telling everyone about his business plan and asking if they have any connections in the music industry.

jokes.text: Tom, still in the stakeout van, says 'I wanted to see if you could tell' after Leslie apparently didn't notice he was still there.
jokes.setup: Leslie apparently left without noticing Tom was still in the van.
jokes.punchline: Tom has been sitting silently to test Leslie's surveillance awareness — a meta-commentary on her as a stakeout partner.
jokes.explanation: A small comedic beat that works as a light jab at Leslie's focus. Functional but minor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm fine. I don't need help. I can walk to that car myself.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, you can barely stand.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm a man. I can push through the pain. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to sit down for a moment.

jokes.text: Andy tells Tom and Leslie: 'Man, oh, man. So how's Ann? She's doing good? I miss her so much, it's ridiculous.'
jokes.setup: Andy is hanging out in the stakeout van, supposedly to help watch for the marijuana planter.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately pivots from surveillance duty to pining for Ann, asking Tom and Leslie about her — not aware (or not caring) that this is awkward given the context.
jokes.explanation: Andy's casual oversharing about missing Ann while supposedly on a stakeout is good character comedy. The irony that Ann is currently on a date nearby adds an uncomfortable layer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So... that happened.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Yeah. We should probably talk about this.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I mean, we work together, so—

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: We're gonna get fired, aren't we? We're both getting fired. I'm gonna lose my job, my house, and I'll probably end up living in a box under the Ramsett Park overpass.

jokes.text: Leslie, when Andy asks how Ann is doing: 'Doing good tonight. She's out on a... Ann is great. And I bet she really misses you.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks about Ann; Leslie almost reveals Ann is on a date before catching herself.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's near-slip ('She's out on a...') and recovery ('Ann is great. And I bet she really misses you') is a painful piece of cringe comedy — the false consolation to Andy.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy. Leslie's desperate pivot to 'And I bet she really misses you' as compensation for the almost-slip is both kindly meant and deeply ironic given Ann is on a date a few feet away.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know plants! I have a very extensive knowledge of botanical species and their care requirements. I've read numerous gardening books and I've been maintaining a thriving indoor garden for years!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Those plants died because of external factors completely beyond my control, not because of anything I did wrong!

jokes.text: Andy enthusiastically eats the candy necklace in one go: 'Oh, my God!' / Leslie: 'You know there's a string in there.' / Andy: 'Not in this one.' / [He begins bouncing off the walls from the sugar rush]
jokes.setup: Leslie offers Andy candy necklaces from the stakeout supplies.
jokes.punchline: Andy eats the whole necklace — string and all, apparently — and then gets an instant sugar rush described in rapid-fire confessional ('Sugar high. Sugar hit high. Sugar slam.')
jokes.explanation: Andy's immediate sugar high from a candy necklace is funny physical comedy that also serves as a dark echo of the marijuana-high storyline. 'Not in this one' about the string is a great quick line. The rapid sugar-rush confessional ('Sugar slam') is fun.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: You only care about this because you want to be the hero of the story.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That is... not true. I care about the park. And the community. And...

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: And being the hero.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: ...okay, yes. But is that so bad?

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: No. Actually, it's kind of great.

jokes.text: Andy, coming down from the sugar rush: 'I'm in.' / Ron, from offscreen: 'Bring me back two cheeseburgers and a green tea.'
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests getting Andy something more substantial to eat after the sugar crash.
jokes.punchline: Ron is apparently still nearby (or being consulted) and immediately takes the opportunity to place a specific food order: two cheeseburgers and a green tea.
jokes.explanation: Ron's unsolicited food order is perfectly Ron — he sees an opportunity and takes it with zero ceremony. 'Two cheeseburgers and a green tea' is funny because the green tea is a surprisingly delicate addition to the two cheeseburgers.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Leslie is... she's got this energy, you know? She's very... enthusiastic.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: And she's smart. Very smart. And determined. She really commits to things.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: She's got great... she's very... I mean, physically, she's...

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just saying I find her very attractive and it's making this really hard.

jokes.text: Mark's elaborate pretend refusal of Ann's nightcap invite: 'I would like you to now please invite me in for a nightcap. Not a chance. No. Just watch what I'm gonna do. Ask me in for a nightcap. Will you come in for a nightcap? Yes, I will. No, no, damn. Drats, I was gonna plan to not.'
jokes.setup: After a good date, Mark sets up an elaborate bit about being a gentleman by planning to decline Ann's invitation.
jokes.punchline: Mark completely fails his own bit — he immediately says 'Yes, I will' when Ann asks, then catches himself with 'Drats, I was gonna plan to not' — the self-sabotage of his gentleman routine.
jokes.explanation: A solid romantic comedy beat that reveals Mark's genuine interest while making him slightly bumbling. The bit is a little overlong but the self-sabotage ('Drats, I was gonna plan to not') is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That was such an amazing day! We really bonded out there. I feel like we're basically best friends now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's great. Hey, I should probably get going though.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Already? But I was thinking we could grab dinner and talk about our feelings and dreams!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I really can't. I have to... I have plans.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, what kind of plans? Because I'm free all week. We could do a whole trip! Remember how fun that was?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no—very important plans. Work stuff. I gotta go right now actually.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You seem anxious. Is this about your feelings? We can talk through this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not anxious, I'm just—LESLIE, I have to leave. Like, immediately.

jokes.text: Mark spots a man 'breaking into that van' — which is actually Tom trying to get back into the stakeout van.
jokes.setup: Mark and Ann are outside her house after their date when Mark notices Tom trying to get into the van.
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Tom is locked out of his own van; Mark doesn't, creating dramatic irony that will spiral into Tom's arrest.
jokes.explanation: A solid plot-driven comedic setup. The audience knowing what Mark doesn't creates situational irony. Functions more as plot mechanics than pure comedy but has good comedic payoff downstream.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We weren't arrested, we were just detained for questioning.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: You were arrested.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I just like being nearby. That way if she wants me back, I could be at her house in two seconds, before she changes her mind.'
jokes.setup: Andy has revealed he's been nearby Ann's house by living in the pit.
jokes.punchline: His logic — being positioned to intercept Ann before she changes her mind — is simultaneously sweet and deeply concerning, delivered with total earnestness.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent character comedy moment. The phrase 'before she changes her mind' is the key — it reveals Andy believes the problem isn't Ann not wanting him back, just a timing issue. The earnest commitment to this profoundly flawed romantic strategy is deeply Andy. Strong craft and character integration.

jokes.text: Leslie accidentally reveals Ann is dating someone: 'Is she? / What? / Is she dating somebody else? / What? / She's dating somebody else? / I didn't say that. / Who is she dating? / Nobody. Mark.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Andy he might not be healthy living nearby Ann, implying she might be moving on.
jokes.punchline: Andy's increasingly frantic questioning and Leslie's increasingly desperate denials escalate rapidly until she just blurts out 'Mark' — a perfect comedic unraveling.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating cringe comedy. The rapid-fire back-and-forth is perfectly structured — Andy's relentless questioning exploits every gap Leslie leaves, and her final 'Nobody. Mark.' is a brilliantly defeated capitulation. The rhythm and timing of this exchange make it one of the episode's highlights.

jokes.text: Tom to the police officer: 'It's okay, my name's Tom Haverford. I work for the Parks Department.' / Officer: 'Why don't you jimmy your way out and show me some ID?' / Tom: 'I just told you my ID, so what's the crime here? Parking while Indian?'
jokes.setup: Tom has been caught trying to break into the van and is now being questioned by a police officer.
jokes.punchline: 'Parking while Indian?' — Tom invokes racial profiling with a riff on 'driving while Black,' turning the situation into a dark-comedy commentary on policing.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy that connects to Tom's earlier monologue about systemic racism. 'Parking while Indian' is a clever and pointed riff that works as both comedy and commentary. The officer's response ('There's no stereotypes about Indians sitting in vehicles') adds an unintentionally defensive layer.

jokes.text: Tom, after being shown his ID is actually being examined: 'Nice job, Paul Blart. Why don't you head back to the mall, make sure nobody's breaking into lady-foot locker?'
jokes.setup: The officer is reviewing Tom's ID and maintaining authority.
jokes.punchline: Tom insults the officer by comparing him to Paul Blart: Mall Cop — a culturally specific, cutting insult that also gets the store name wrong ('lady-foot locker' vs. 'foot locker').
jokes.explanation: Tom's pop-culture insults are very on-brand, and Paul Blart is a well-chosen target for belittling a cop. The 'lady-foot locker' detail is a nice small comedy error that suggests Tom's mind is working faster than his accuracy.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I'll step out of your mama's van.' [followed by escalating physical struggle with the officer]
jokes.setup: The officer threatens Tom with arrest for disorderly conduct and tells him to step out of the van.
jokes.punchline: 'I'll step out of your mama's van' — Tom's middle-school-level comeback in a high-stakes situation is an absurd escalation of his confrontational mode.
jokes.explanation: The 'your mama' joke is deliberately juvenile — that's the point. Tom regresses to playground insults when cornered. It works because of the mismatch between the adult stakes (potential arrest) and the childish response.

jokes.text: Tom gets sprayed by motion-sensor sprinklers in the van area while being arrested.
jokes.setup: Tom is being forcibly removed from the van by the officer.
jokes.punchline: The motion sensors trigger sprinklers, adding soaking humiliation to Tom's arrest.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy escalation — the sprinklers add insult to injury during the arrest. A reliable laugh but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Leslie threatens the cop with 'I could have Ron Swanson down here. Kicking down your doors.' — cop asks which branch of government. Long pause. 'Parks and Recreation.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to use bureaucratic muscle to help Tom. She builds up Ron Swanson as a fearsome government authority.
jokes.punchline: The cop asks which branch of government. The [15:52] → [15:57] gap is a beat of Leslie realizing the answer is going to undermine her threat. Then: 'Parks and Recreation.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect: Leslie builds Ron Swanson up as a fearsome authority figure ('Kicking down your doors'), the cop asks a reasonable question, there's an implied beat as Leslie realizes her answer will destroy her credibility — and then she delivers it anyway with full conviction: 'Parks and Recreation.' The follow-up 'Do I stutter?' after the [16:04] gap is a perfect button — Leslie refusing to acknowledge that her answer has undermined her threat. The character integration is exceptional: only Leslie Knope would genuinely believe the Parks Department is a threatening entity.

jokes.text: 'Do I stutter?' — Leslie's defiant follow-up after revealing she's from Parks and Recreation.
jokes.setup: The cop is presumably unimpressed that Leslie's threat came from the Parks Department.
jokes.punchline: 'Do I stutter?' — Leslie's complete refusal to acknowledge that 'Parks and Recreation' is not a threatening entity, delivered with maximum conviction.
jokes.explanation: Three words that are among the best in the episode. 'Do I stutter?' is a power move that makes zero sense given that Leslie has just said 'Parks and Recreation' — but Leslie's absolute commitment to the threat is the whole joke. The character integration is near-perfect: Leslie's unwavering belief in the importance and dignity of her work, even when that work is parks management, is the core of her character.

jokes.text: Cop reveals Tom's van contained 'an enormous amount of manure, and a very inappropriate amount of candy.'
jokes.setup: The cop is explaining why Tom seems like a pervert — they searched the van.
jokes.punchline: 'A very inappropriate amount of candy' — the phrase 'inappropriate amount of candy' is a callback to the stakeout supply list and the Andy sugar-rush scene, now recontextualized as evidence of perversion.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful callback payoff. The candy from the stakeout supplies that seemed innocuous is now 'a very inappropriate amount of candy' — a phrase that sounds deeply sinister in the context of an arrest. The episode has been patiently setting up this callback since the [04:44] supply reveal.

jokes.text: Leslie explains to Officer Dave why there's photography equipment, manure, and candy in the van: 'I brought the candy, a lot of it, because I love it.'
jokes.setup: Officer Dave lists the disturbing items found in the van — photography equipment, photos of people on a date, manure, and 'a very inappropriate amount of candy.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie addresses each concern in turn, but 'I brought the candy, a lot of it, because I love it' is delivered as a completely sufficient explanation — no defense, just declaration.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Leslie line. The setup (the officer listing all the disturbing contents) makes the candy seem like part of something sinister. Leslie's explanation — not even an apology, just 'because I love it' — is the perfect response. The economy is exceptional: it explains nothing while explaining everything about Leslie's character. Justifies the 8+ craft score.

jokes.text: Leslie's full confession to Officer Dave: 'My best friend was going on a date with my ex-lover. It's been a very long night.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to explain the photography equipment and the photos of Ann and Mark on a date.
jokes.punchline: 'It's been a very long night' — the understatement that caps a confession involving surveillance, marijuana, candy hoarding, and romantic jealousy.
jokes.explanation: The understatement of 'It's been a very long night' works beautifully as a self-aware summary. Leslie's willingness to confess everything with weary dignity is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Prison changes a man. I think he'll wanna see a familiar face when he gets back on the outside.'
jokes.setup: Leslie insists on waiting for Tom at the police station rather than going home.
jokes.punchline: Leslie describes Tom's brief police detention as a prison sentence that will fundamentally alter him — treating a misdemeanor holding as a life-changing incarceration.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie overstatement. Her treating a brief police hold as a prison term — complete with talk of 'the outside' — is both funny and touching, because she genuinely means it. The dramatic register applied to a minor situation is classic Parks and Rec.

jokes.text: April arrives to drive Ron home: 'Yo. I had to wait till my dad fell asleep so I could steal his keys. You ready?' / Ron: 'I was born ready.'
jokes.setup: Ron needs a ride to the hospital.
jokes.punchline: April, a government intern, had to sneak out of her parents' house to help Ron — and Ron's 'I was born ready' is a magnificently stoic response to needing emergency medical help via a teenager who stole her dad's car.
jokes.explanation: 'I was born ready' in the context of needing emergency hernia treatment via a teenage car thief is a great deadpan moment. April's casual lawbreaking on Ron's behalf also reveals their odd-couple dynamic.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I'm Ron [bleep] Swanson.' [as he tries to get into April's car and clearly struggles with the hernia]
jokes.setup: Ron is about to get into the car to go to the hospital.
jokes.punchline: Ron declares his identity — name-drop bleep — as a statement of toughness while visibly struggling with basic movement due to the hernia. The declaration and the physical reality are in complete opposition.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most quotable and iconic moment. 'I'm Ron [bleep] Swanson' is the perfect encapsulation of the character: utterly self-assured, name-drops himself with the bleep as emphasis, delivered while physically compromised. The bleeping of his own middle name elevates this to legendary territory — it implies both profanity and a kind of self-mythologizing. High craft score is fully justified.

jokes.text: Mark and Ann approaching Ann's door: Ann: 'I really don't think you should invite me in. Terrible things happened last time.'
jokes.setup: Mark and Ann are at her door after their date.
jokes.punchline: Mark — who is supposed to be being a gentleman — preemptively requests not to be invited in, attributing 'terrible things' to last time, which is ironic given his history with her.
jokes.explanation: A serviceable romantic comedy beat. 'Terrible things happened last time' is doing some light work implying their sexual history while playing demure. Functional rather than inspired.

jokes.text: Ann: 'You kind of kissed me.' / Mark: 'Yes, I did, and now we both have herpes.'
jokes.setup: Ann points out that Mark just kissed her despite his 'terrible things happened last time' position.
jokes.punchline: Mark's response to being caught in a romantic moment is an immediate dark joke: 'now we both have herpes' — deflecting intimacy with STI humor.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed dark joke. The setup (Ann's mild observation) is immediately met with maximum deflection. The herpes line is darkly funny and characterizes Mark as someone who uses edgy humor as emotional distance. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Tom is released from custody and finds Leslie waiting with his chocolate. Tom: 'It's not your chocolate. Don't... get your hands off that.' Leslie, caught eating it: responds sheepishly.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been waiting loyally for Tom at the police station.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has been eating Tom's chocolate while waiting — undermining her noble vigil.
jokes.explanation: A small callback to Leslie's love of candy/sugar. Reinforces the character trait and provides a nice comedic note to her devoted wait. Functional and warm.

jokes.text: Officer Dave offers Leslie his coat, then immediately takes it back: 'Really? / Actually, no. I need that for my uniform.'
jokes.setup: Officer Dave gives Leslie his coat as a gentlemanly gesture.
jokes.punchline: He immediately reclaims it when he realizes it's his uniform jacket — a practical reconsideration that deflates the romantic gesture.
jokes.explanation: A sweet and simple beat. The rapid reversal from generosity to practicality is endearing and reveals Dave as a likeable character. The comedy is mild but charming.

jokes.text: Andy, when the marijuana has disappeared from the garden: 'So where's that marijuana at?' / Officer Dave: 'It's down in the garden.' / Dave: 'Good meeting you, man. Should grab a drink sometime.'
jokes.setup: The stakeout has ended; Officer Dave is releasing Tom and wrapping up.
jokes.punchline: Andy casually asks the cop about the weed's location, and the officer just as casually tells him — then immediately follows with a friendly social invitation, as if they've bonded.
jokes.explanation: A fun absurdist beat: the police officer and the man living in a pit bond over casual marijuana chat. Andy's directness cuts through all social norms and somehow works.

jokes.text: Tom, to Leslie after a beat: 'Mark's an idiot. You could do a lot better than him. Forget about him.' / Leslie: 'Thanks, Tom.' / Tom: 'I didn't mean me. Keep it in your pants, Knope.'
jokes.setup: Tom is comforting Leslie about Ann and Mark's date.
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't mean me. Keep it in your pants, Knope.' — Tom pre-emptively clarifies that his supportive comment wasn't an offer, hilariously putting the 'overstep' on Leslie rather than himself.
jokes.explanation: Excellent end-of-episode Tom moment. The structure is tight: the sweet setup (Tom's supportive comment) and then the immediate reversal ('I didn't mean me') flips the sentiment perfectly. 'Keep it in your pants, Knope' applied to Leslie is deeply funny — it implies Leslie was the one making it weird, which is both unfair and perfectly in character for Tom. Quotable and character-revealing. Justifies 8+ score.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I hope Ann and Mark got home okay.' Tom: '...That's all that matters. That Ann is home, and she's okay. And that Mark is also okay, and he is in his home. Just important that they're both in their homes.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she hopes Ann and Mark got home okay.
jokes.punchline: The lengthy qualification — emphasizing they are each in their own separate homes — reveals Leslie's very specific hope that the date did not progress past the front door. The repetition and over-specification is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's denial working against her in real-time. The over-specification ('he is in his home,' 'just important that they're both in their homes') reveals exactly what she's worried about while ostensibly expressing neutral well-wishes. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Officer Dave, examining the garden: 'You don't think I know the difference between carrots and marijuana?' [holding up what are clearly carrots]
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to show Officer Dave the marijuana, but it appears to have been replaced with or mistaken for carrots.
jokes.punchline: Dave insists on his drug identification expertise while holding up carrots — a callback to the original carrot/marijuana confusion that opened the episode.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the episode's central plant identification confusion. The irony of a cop insisting he knows marijuana while holding carrots is funny. The closing of this narrative loop is well-handled.

jokes.text: Officer Dave accuses Leslie of inventing the weed story to spy on Ann's date: 'You made up a story about weed so you could stake out their date. / I did not. There actually was weed here. / It's okay. I think it's kind of cute.'
jokes.setup: Dave has pieced together the real motive behind the stakeout.
jokes.punchline: 'I think it's kind of cute' — Dave's gentle re-framing of Leslie's denial-wrapped obsession as endearing is the pivot that makes this a romantic comedy beat.
jokes.explanation: A warm comedic moment that also advances Leslie's new romantic subplot. The comedy of Dave finding her chaos 'kind of cute' is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Officer Dave's extended confessional about Leslie: 'I like Miss Knope. I gotta say when I first met her, I didn't care much for her, because, like 99% of the people in any given day of my life, she was very belligerent and disagreeable. Miss Knope was attractive to me as a man. I was attracted to her in her demeanor. I was attracted to her in a sexual manner that was appropriate. I don't want to talk about this anymore.'
jokes.setup: The show cuts to Dave's talking-head confessional about Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Dave's painfully over-qualified statement about his attraction — 'in a sexual manner that was appropriate' — and his immediate shutdown ('I don't want to talk about this anymore') is a perfect comedic implosion of self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest moments. The escalating qualifications — 'attracted to her in her demeanor,' then the defensive 'in a sexual manner that was appropriate' — build to the perfect shutdown. The phrase 'in a sexual manner that was appropriate' is both hilarious and deeply human: Dave is so worried about being inappropriate that his very disclaimer is awkward. 'I don't want to talk about this anymore' is a perfect button. Justifies 8+ craft score.

jokes.text: Tom spots something on TV: 'Oh, my God, I can't believe this is on!' / Leslie: 'I wonder if mini golf is open. Home!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is demanding to go home; Tom is driving.
jokes.punchline: Tom is distracted by something on TV (presumably visible from the road), and Leslie imagines mini golf as an alternative — the mundane tangents during an emotionally significant moment are funny.
jokes.explanation: A small character beat. Functional filler rather than a strong joke, but Leslie's 'Home!' as a final command is a good button.

jokes.text: Tom, to Ann and Mark: 'Ann-danawicz, what are you guys doing? Eating? Love it. Just wanted to thank you for having me arrested as a pervert the other night. That was cool. Peace.'
jokes.setup: Tom stops by to address Ann and Mark after his arrest.
jokes.punchline: Tom's hyper-casual, breezy delivery of a genuine grievance — 'Just wanted to thank you... That was cool. Peace.' — uses ironic politeness to maximize passive aggression.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom moment. The structure is tight: the absurdly casual setup ('Eating? Love it.') followed by the grievance with faux-gratitude ('Just wanted to thank you'), ending with 'That was cool. Peace.' The rhythm and delivery make this one of Tom's best lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Ann: 'We didn't think you were a pervert. We thought you were a criminal.' / Leslie (in confessional): 'For the record, I still actually kind of think he's a pervert.'
jokes.setup: Tom protests being thought of as a pervert.
jokes.punchline: Ann corrects the record ('criminal, not pervert'), and then Leslie's confessional immediately undercuts Ann's defense.
jokes.explanation: A great final joke for the episode. Ann's defense of Tom is immediately and hilariously undercut by Leslie's talking-head aside. The structure — public defense followed by private betrayal — is a classic mockumentary move, executed cleanly. 'For the record, I still actually kind of think he's a pervert' is a perfect closer.

tmdb_overview: While tending to the new community garden, Leslie and Tom discover someone has planted marijuana among the vegetables. In an effort to catch the people responsible, they pull an all-night stakeout. With Leslie's permission, Ann decides to go on a date with Mark.
insight: Leslie's enthusiasm drives 80-plus comedy through pure character-based absurdism and deadpan restraint.
